cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q1] Ned-Leaks scandals: the Netherlands turns out to be a tax haven whose schemes distort competition in the EU. Commission President Peter Niederknaaken, formerly Dutch Minister of Finance, comes under fire. Does the European Parliament have the power to remove Commission President Niederknaaken? (2 points)
cards.a:
No — the EP can only censure the whole Commission, not the President alone.
• Art 17(8) TEU: Commission responsible to the EP as a body; censure carried → all members incl. President resign.
• Art 234 TFEU: two-thirds of votes cast, representing a majority of component Members.
• Individual compulsory retirement: only the CJEU, on Council or Commission application (Art 247 TFEU).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q2] In connection with the Ned-Leaks scandals, an EU legal act is issued in the form of a regulation. Can it nevertheless be transposed into national law? (2 points)
cards.a:
No — a regulation needs no transposition and must not be transposed.
• Art 288(2) TFEU: general application, binding in its entirety, directly applicable in all Member States (unlike directives, Art 288(3)).
• Re-enacting it nationally would conceal its EU nature and endanger uniform application → infringement (Variola 34/73).
• Allowed: implementing measures it requires (authorities, penalties; Art 291(1) TFEU).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q3] What is the difference between delegated acts and implementing acts? (3 points)
cards.a:
Delegated acts supplement/amend legislation (EP/Council control); implementing acts ensure uniform implementation (Member State control).
• Art 290(1) TFEU: a legislative act delegates to the Commission non-legislative acts of general application supplementing/amending non-essential elements; objectives, content, scope, duration explicitly defined.
• Art 290(2): EP or Council may revoke or object.
• Art 291(1)–(2) TFEU: Member States implement; where uniform conditions are needed, the binding act confers powers on the Commission (exceptionally Council).
• Art 291(3): control by Member States (comitology, Reg 182/2011).
• 290 adds/changes norms; 291 specifies without amending (C-88/14).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q4] Why and to what extent is the primacy of EU law a conflict-resolution rule? (3 points)
cards.a:
Primacy decides which conflicting norm applies in the case — primacy of application, not validity.
• Why: EU and national law are autonomous, interlocking orders; uniform, effective application requires EU law to prevail (Costa v ENEL 6/64).
• Effect: national court disapplies the conflicting rule (Simmenthal 106/77); it is not void and still applies outside EU law (IN.CO.GE.'90 C-10/97).
• Extent: only a genuine conflict (conform interpretation first) with a directly effective EU rule (Popławski II C-573/17).
• State must still amend its law (Commission v France 167/73).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q5] How does the Court of Justice justify the primacy of EU law over national law? (3 points)
cards.a:
No Treaty article (only Declaration 17): CJEU derives primacy from the nature of EU law (Costa v ENEL 6/64).
• Own legal order: the Treaty became an integral part of national legal systems, binding their courts (Costa; Van Gend en Loos 26/62).
• Transfer of sovereignty: states permanently limited sovereign rights → no later unilateral national measure prevails.
• Uniformity: EU law's effect cannot vary between states without jeopardising Treaty aims (Art 4(3) TEU; Art 18 TFEU).
• Art 288(2) TFEU: regulations' direct applicability would otherwise be meaningless.

cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q6] Does EU law enjoy primacy over national constitutional law according to the Court of Justice? Discuss, with reference to case law, and explain how the Treaties take account of national constitutional identity. (3 points)
cards.a:
Yes — for the CJEU EU law prevails even over national constitutions.
• Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70): EU acts cannot be measured against national constitutional rights; rights protected as general principles of EU law.
• Melloni (C-399/11): no higher national constitutional standard where EU law is exhaustive (Art 53 Charter).
• Art 4(2) TEU: Union respects national identity in fundamental constitutional structures → justification ground (Sayn-Wittgenstein C-208/09), not a licence to disapply EU law (RS C-430/21).
• Contra: national constitutional courts claim rights/identity/ultra vires review (BVerfG Solange, Lisbon, PSPP).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q7] What is an ultra vires act? (2 points)
cards.a:
Act of a Union institution beyond the competences conferred by the Treaties.
• Conferral: Art 5(1)–(2) TEU; non-conferred competences stay with Member States (Art 4(1) TEU); institutions act within their powers (Art 13(2) TEU).
• EU view: only the CJEU declares it invalid (Arts 263(2), 267 TFEU; Foto-Frost 314/85).
• National view: BVerfG review if manifest and structurally significant (Honeywell 2010, PSPP 2020).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q8] Van Gend en Loos (1963): the Netherlands raised the customs duty on a chemical imported from Germany from 3% to 8%, contrary to the standstill clause in Art 12 EEC (now Art 30 TFEU). The Dutch and Belgian governments argued that only the Commission or another Member State could enforce the Treaty, through infringement proceedings. What were the Court's main arguments for direct effect, and why did it reject the governments' objection? (4 points)
cards.a:
Treaty's spirit, scheme and wording create a new legal order including individuals; infringement proceedings don't exclude individual enforcement.
• Spirit: common market concerns individuals; preamble refers to 'peoples', citizens participate via EP/ECOSOC → more than mutual state obligations.
• Scheme: preliminary reference (now Art 267 TFEU) presupposes nationals invoking EU law before national courts.
• New legal order: states limited sovereign rights; rights also arise from clearly defined obligations on states.
• Wording: Art 12 EEC was clear, unconditional and negative, needing no implementing measure → directly effective.
• Objection: Arts 169/170 EEC (now 258/259 TFEU) not exclusive; vigilance of individuals adds effective supervision → Van Gend could rely on Art 12.

cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q9] What is meant by the "autonomy" of Union law, and how does the Court of Justice justify and protect it? (2 points)
cards.a:
EU law is an independent legal order, separate from international and national law; the CJEU alone decides its meaning.
• Justified: 'new legal order' (Van Gend en Loos 26/62), 'own legal system' (Costa v ENEL 6/64) → not measured against national law.
• Protected: CJEU interpretive monopoly (Art 19(1) TEU, Art 267 TFEU); exclusive EU dispute settlement (Art 344 TFEU; Achmea C-284/16, Opinion 2/13).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 1 Q10] What are the conditions for direct effect of Union law? Do they depend on the kind of legal act and on the relationship in which the provision is invoked (vertical/horizontal)? (3 points)
cards.a:
Clear, precise, unconditional; yes — invocability depends on act and relationship.
• Van Gend en Loos (26/62): sufficiently clear and precise, unconditional (no discretionary implementing measure needed) → confers rights.
• Act (Art 288 TFEU): Treaty articles, regulations (288(2)), decisions (288(4); Grad 9/70) yes; directives (288(3)) only after the deadline if not/wrongly transposed (Ratti 148/78).
• Vertical: against the state.
• Horizontal: Treaty articles binding private parties (Defrenne II, Art 157 TFEU) and regulations; never directives (Marshall I 152/84, Faccini Dori C-91/92); no inverse vertical effect (Kolpinghuis 80/86).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 2 Q1] A Belgian environmental association asks the Belgian Conseil d'État to annul a Walloon decree of 9 April 1992 on hazardous waste, arguing that it conflicts with Directive 91/689. Belgium adopted the decree after the directive, but before its transposition period expired. The decree exempts certain waste operations from the permit requirement the directive imposes. Can the association rely on EU law? (4 points)
cards.a:
Yes — not on the directive's direct effect, but on the duty not to seriously compromise its result before the deadline (Inter-Environnement Wallonie, C-129/96).
• No direct effect: vertical direct effect requires an expired transposition deadline (Ratti) → directive not invocable as such.
• Art 4(3) TEU + Art 288(3) TFEU: before the deadline Member States need not comply, but must not adopt provisions liable seriously to compromise the result prescribed (IEW).
• Test: does it present itself as definitive transposition; concrete effects; duration.
• Application: a definitive decree exempting operations from permits can seriously compromise the result → for the Conseil d'État to assess; if so, it annuls; may refer (Art 267 TFEU).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 2 Q2] Can directives have direct effect between private parties (horizontal direct effect)? Give the reasons for the Court of Justice's position and explain the ways around it. (4 points)
cards.a:
No — a directive cannot of itself impose obligations on an individual (Marshall I; Faccini Dori); direct effect is only vertical, against the state (Ratti).
• Reasons: binding only on "each Member State to which it is addressed" (Art 288(3) TFEU); estoppel hits the defaulting state, not a private party; otherwise no difference from regulations (Art 288(2) TFEU); legal certainty.
• Workaround 1 — broad notion of the state: state as employer (Marshall I), emanations of the state (Foster).
• Workaround 2 — consistent interpretation (Von Colson; Marleasing), never contra legem.
• Workaround 3 — directive expressing a general principle/Charter right (Mangold; Kücükdeveci); incidental effect (CIA Security; Unilever).
• Last resort: state liability (Francovich).

cards.q: [Set A · Case 2 Q3] What is meant by the "indirect effect" of directives? Explain its legal basis, its scope and its limits. (3 points)
cards.a:
The duty of national courts and authorities to interpret national law as far as possible in conformity with a directive (Von Colson; Marleasing).
• Basis: Art 288(3) TFEU + Art 4(3) TEU bind all state authorities, including courts (Von Colson, 14/83).
• Scope: all national law, earlier or later (Marleasing), also between private parties; all recognised methods (Pfeiffer); from the transposition deadline; provision need not be directly effective.
• Limits: never contra legem (Adeneler); legal certainty → cannot create or aggravate criminal liability (Kolpinghuis).
• Otherwise → state liability (Francovich).

cards.q: [Set B · Case 1 Q1] The Union legislator wants to adopt a directive harmonising the framework under which national competition authorities enforce Union and national competition law (independence, resources, powers), while ensuring the proper functioning of the internal market and of the European Competition Network. What is the proper legal basis for this directive, and which procedure follows from it? (3 points)
cards.a:
Art 103 + Art 114 TFEU (like ECN+ Directive 2019/1) → ordinary legislative procedure (Art 294 TFEU).
• Competence: exclusive (Art 3(1)(b) TFEU), but catalogue ≠ legal basis.
• Art 103(1) TFEU: Council, on Commission proposal after consulting the EP, gives effect to Arts 101–102 → alone: mere consultation.
• Art 114(1) TFEU: approximation for the internal market (authorities' independence, resources, powers) → OLP.
• Choice by aim and content (Titanium dioxide, C-300/89); two inseparable aims → dual basis if procedures compatible: Council QMV under both → OLP absorbs consultation.

cards.q: [Set B · Case 1 Q2] Explain the individual steps of the ordinary legislative procedure, including the majorities and time limits. (5 points)
cards.a:
Arts 289(1), 294 TFEU: proposal → 1st, 2nd reading → conciliation → 3rd reading; EP and Council co-decide.
• Proposal: Commission (Art 294(2)); Council amends only unanimously (Art 293(1)).
• 1st reading, no time limit: EP position (simple majority); Council approves (QMV) → adopted, otherwise own position (Art 294(3)–(6)).
• 2nd reading, EP within 3 months: approves/silent → adopted; rejects or amends by majority of component members (Art 294(7)). Council within 3 months approves all amendments (QMV; unanimity on amendments Commission rejects) → adopted (Art 294(8)–(9)).
• Otherwise Conciliation Committee within 6 weeks (Council + equal number of MEPs): joint text within 6 weeks (Council QMV, EP-delegation majority), else fails (Art 294(10)–(12)).
• 3rd reading within 6 weeks: EP (majority of votes cast) and Council (QMV), else fails (Art 294(13)); extensions +1 month/+2 weeks (Art 294(14)); OJ (Art 297(1)).

cards.q: [Set B · Case 1 Q3] What is enhanced cooperation? (3 points)
cards.a:
At least nine Member States may, as a last resort, use EU institutions to adopt acts binding only themselves (Art 20 TEU; Arts 326–334 TFEU).
• Conditions: non-exclusive competences (Art 20(1) TEU); last resort, nine states (Art 20(2) TEU); internal market, cohesion intact (Art 326 TFEU); non-participants respected, open to all (Arts 327–328 TFEU).
• Authorisation: Council (QMV), Commission proposal, EP consent (Art 329(1) TFEU).
• Effects: only participants vote (Art 20(3) TEU, Art 330 TFEU); acts bind only them (Art 20(4) TEU).
• Examples: Rome III, unitary patent, EPPO.

cards.q: [Set B · Case 1 Q4] What constitutes the principle of decentralised enforcement of EU law? (3 points)
cards.a:
As a rule Member States, not the Union, implement and enforce EU law; direct EU enforcement is the exception (explicit legal basis).
• Authorities: adopt measures implementing binding Union acts (Art 291(1) TFEU; Art 4(3) TEU); EU implementing powers only for uniform conditions (Art 291(2)).
• Courts: ordinary EU-law courts → direct effect, primacy (Van Gend, Costa, Simmenthal); effective remedies (Art 19(1) subpara 2 TEU, Art 47 Charter); Art 267 TFEU references.
• National procedure within equivalence and effectiveness (Rewe; Comet).
• Commission supervises (Art 17(1) TEU; Arts 258–260 TFEU).

cards.q: [Set B · Case 1 Q5] Give examples of own (direct) enforcement of Union law. (2 points)
cards.a:
Competition, trade, directly managed funds, EU administration — exceptions, each with explicit legal basis.
• Competition: Commission decisions/fines under Arts 101–102 (Art 105 TFEU, Reg 1/2003), mergers, state aid (Art 108(2) TFEU), DMA.
• Trade: Commission anti-dumping/countervailing duties (Art 207 TFEU).
• Funds/research under direct management; EU staff and budget (Arts 336, 317 TFEU).
• Not customs: exclusive (Art 3 TFEU), but collected nationally.

cards.q: [Set B · Case 1 Q6] What is meant by the principle of procedural autonomy? (3 points)
cards.a:
Absent EU procedural rules, each Member State designates the courts and procedure for EU-law claims, limited by equivalence and effectiveness (Rewe; Comet).
• Equivalence: no less favourable than similar domestic claims.
• Effectiveness: exercise of EU rights not practically impossible or excessively difficult (Impact); reasonable time limits are fine (Rewe).
• Basis: Arts 4(3), 19(1) subpara 2 TEU, Art 47 Charter → EU law may itself demand a remedy: interim relief (Factortame I), damages (Francovich).
• EU procedural rules prevail where they exist; references follow Art 267 TFEU itself.

cards.q: [Set B · Case 2 Q1] The Irish Merchant Shipping Act 2020 introduced nationality and residence requirements for registering fishing vessels as Irish; Spanish-owned fishing companies were then barred from Irish waters. They sought judicial review of the Act's compatibility with the EU Treaties (freedom of establishment) and interim relief suspending the Act until final judgment. Under Irish common law, courts cannot suspend Acts of Parliament by way of interim relief. Can the fishers rely on EU law to obtain interim relief? (3 points)
cards.a:
Yes — a national court must set aside a national rule that is the sole obstacle to interim relief in a case governed by EU law (Factortame I, C-213/89).
• Primacy: every court disapplies national rules impairing full effectiveness of EU law (Simmenthal; Art 4(3) TEU).
• Effective judicial protection (Art 19(1) subpara 2 TEU, Art 47 Charter) → interim relief must protect the claimed Art 49 TFEU right.
• Application: Irish court disapplies common-law bar, applies ordinary interim-relief conditions; may refer (Art 267 TFEU).
• Later: damages (Factortame III).

cards.q: [Set B · Case 2 Q2] Can a claim for damages against Member States for breach of Union law be based on Article 340(2) TFEU? (2 points)
cards.a:
No — Art 340(2) TFEU covers only the Union's own non-contractual liability.
• Art 340(2) TFEU: the Union makes good damage caused by its institutions or servants → action against the Union before the EU Courts (Art 268 TFEU).
• Member State liability is an unwritten general principle (Francovich; Art 4(3) TEU) → national courts; Art 340(2) only inspired its conditions (Brasserie du Pêcheur).

cards.q: [Set B · Case 2 Q3] Can an individual claim damages from a Member State for a breach of EU law? On what legal basis, under which conditions, and before which court? (4 points)
cards.a:
Yes — state liability (Francovich), claimed before the national courts if the Brasserie du Pêcheur/Factortame III conditions are met.
• Basis: unwritten general principle inherent in the Treaties — effectiveness of EU law, protection of individual rights (Francovich); Art 4(3) TEU, Art 19(1) subpara 2 TEU; not Art 340(2) TFEU (Union only).
• Conditions: (1) the Member State breaches a rule intended to confer rights on individuals; (2) the breach is sufficiently serious = manifest and grave disregard of discretion (non-transposition per se, Dillenkofer); (3) damage and a direct causal link.
• Any state organ counts: legislature, administration, last-instance court (Köbler).
• Court: national courts under national procedure, subject to equivalence and effectiveness.

cards.q: [Set B · Case 2 Q4] What are the consequences of a breach of the obligation to refer a question to the Court of Justice? (3 points)
cards.a:
The Member State breaches EU law → infringement proceedings and state liability; in Austria also a breach of the lawful-judge right.
• Duty: last-instance courts must refer (Art 267(3) TFEU) unless CILFIT applies (irrelevant, acte éclairé, acte clair).
• Commission may bring Art 258 TFEU proceedings against the Member State (Commission v France, C-416/17).
• State liability for a manifest breach by a last-instance court (Köbler); judgment stays final.
• No individual right to a reference, but in Austria the CJEU is a lawful judge → Art 83(2) B-VG violated.

cards.q: [Set B · Case 2 Q6] Under which conditions can non-privileged claimants file an action for annulment? (3 points)
cards.a:
Natural or legal persons may challenge (Art 263(4) TFEU) an act addressed to them, an act of direct and individual concern, or a regulatory act of direct concern without implementing measures — within two months (Art 263(6)).
• Direct concern: the act directly affects their legal situation, no discretion left to implementers.
• Individual concern (Plaumann): peculiar attributes or circumstances distinguish them from all others like an addressee, e.g. closed class, specific right (Codorniu).
• Regulatory act = non-legislative act of general application (Inuit) → individual concern not needed.

cards.q: [Set B · Case 4 Q1] A and B claim an allowance in lieu of the paid annual leave their deceased husbands had not taken. A's husband worked for a municipality, B's for a private company. German law excluded such claims by spouses, because the leave entitlement lapsed on the worker's death. Article 7 of the Working Time Directive 2003/88 guarantees at least four weeks' paid annual leave. Can both A and B rely on Article 31(2) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights? (4 points)
cards.a:
Yes, both — Art 31(2) Charter is mandatory and unconditional and binds public and private employers alike (Bauer and Willmeroth, C-569/16 and C-570/16).
• Charter = primary law (Art 6(1) TEU) and applies because Germany implements Art 7 Directive 2003/88 (Art 51(1) Charter; Åkerberg Fransson); the allowance does not lapse on death but passes to the heirs.
• First try consistent interpretation of German law; only if contra legem → disapplication.
• A (municipality = state): Art 7 Directive has vertical direct effect, plus Art 31(2) Charter → national rule disapplied.
• B (private employer): directives have no horizontal direct effect (Faccini Dori), but Art 31(2) Charter does → national rule disapplied, B succeeds.

cards.q: [Set C · Q2] Briefly distinguish between the following bodies: the Council of Europe, the European Council, and the Council of the European Union. (3 points)
cards.a:
Only the European Council and the Council are EU institutions (Art 13(1) TEU); the Council of Europe is a separate international organisation.
• Council of Europe: 1949, Strasbourg, 46 states, outside the EU → ECHR and ECtHR.
• European Council (Art 15(1)–(2) TEU): heads of state or government, its President, Commission President → political impetus and priorities; no legislative functions.
• Council (Art 16 TEU): one minister per Member State (Art 16(2)) → legislative and budgetary functions jointly with the EP (Art 16(1)); QMV as a rule (Art 16(3)).

cards.q: [Set C · Q5] Explain the principle of subsidiarity. Where is it regulated? (3 points)
cards.a:
Outside exclusive competence the EU acts only if Member States cannot sufficiently achieve the objective and the EU can do better.
• Regulated in Art 5(3) TEU and Protocol No 2; only non-exclusive competences (not Art 3 TFEU).
• Two cumulative tests: (1) Member States insufficient, centrally, regionally or locally; (2) better at Union level due to scale or effects.
• Governs exercise, not existence, of competences (Art 5(1) TEU).
• National parliaments' reasoned opinions, yellow/orange card (Arts 6–7 Protocol 2); annulment action (Art 8 Protocol 2, Art 263 TFEU).

cards.q: [Set C · Q7] How is a secondary legal act normally adopted? Where is the corresponding procedure regulated? (2 points)

cards.q: [Set C · Q9(a)] Name two so-called 'convergence criteria' that Member States must fulfil if they wish to participate in the third stage of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). (2 points)
cards.a:
Any two of the four criteria (Art 140(1) TFEU, Protocol No 13):
• Price stability: inflation max 1.5 points above the three best Member States.
• Public finances: no excessive deficit under Art 126(6) TFEU (3% / 60% GDP).
• Exchange rate: two years in ERM II within normal margins, no devaluation.
• Long-term interest rates: max 2 points above the three best.

cards.q: [Set D · Case 2(a)] Luís Coentrão, a Portuguese lawyer, wants to emigrate with his family from Lisbon to Austria and open a law firm in Graz. Only Austrian citizens may run a law firm in Austria. Luís believes this violates Union law. (a) Which fundamental freedom could be affected? What indications are there in the facts? Where is this freedom regulated in the Treaties? (3 points)
cards.a:
Freedom of establishment — Art 49 TFEU (Arts 49–55 TFEU).
• Emigrates with family → permanent, stable integration in another MS's economy (Gebhard C-55/94).
• Opens his own law firm → self-employed, not a worker (no subordination, Lawrie-Blum 66/85; Art 45 TFEU out).
• Indefinite, not temporary → not services (Arts 56–57 TFEU, residual, Art 57(1)).
• Portuguese national (Union citizen), Lisbon → Graz → cross-border (Art 49(1)).
• Art 49(2): self-employment under the conditions the host state sets for its own nationals.

Only Austrian citizens may run a law firm in Austria. Luís believes this violates Union law. (b) Is this freedom actually infringed? Argue using the examination structure. (4 points)

Yes — the nationality requirement infringes Art 49 TFEU.
• Scope: Art 49 applies (Union citizen, self-employed, permanent, cross-border); Directive 98/5 even lets EU lawyers practise under their home title.
• Exception Art 51(1) TFEU: lawyers do not exercise official authority (Reyners 2/74) → not excluded.

• Justification: direct discrimination only on Art 52(1) grounds (public policy, security, health) → none; client protection is unwritten (Gebhard) → unavailable.
• Proportionality: anyway not necessary — checking qualifications is milder.
• Result: infringement; Art 49 directly effective (Reyners) → national rule disapplied (primacy).

cards.q: In 2022 the Court of Justice found that State Tarsis had infringed EU waste law by operating illegal landfills. Three years later the landfills are still in operation. What can the Commission do, which sanctions are possible, and how are they set? (3 points)
cards.a:
The Commission can bring Tarsis back before the Court under Art 260(2) TFEU and ask for financial sanctions.
• Art 260(1) TFEU: duty to comply with the 2022 judgment → landfills still running = non-compliance.
• Art 260(2): only a letter of formal notice (chance to submit observations), no reasoned opinion; Commission proposes the amount, Court not bound (unlike Art 260(3)).
• Sanctions: lump sum (past non-compliance) and/or periodic penalty payment (until compliance), both together possible (Commission v France, C-304/02).
• Criteria: seriousness, duration, deterrence, ability to pay.

Yes — inter-state infringement action, Art 259(1) TFEU (Austria v Germany, C-591/17).
• Art 259(2): first bring the matter before the Commission.
• Art 259(3): Commission hears both states, orally and in writing, then gives a reasoned opinion.
• Art 259(4): no opinion within three months does not bar the action, nor does a negative one → Court of Justice, declaratory judgment (Art 260(1)).

cards.q: Which of the following can be challenged under Article 263 TFEU? (a) A Commission letter informing a company that a formal competition investigation against it has been opened. (b) A Commission decision fining a cartel. (c) A Council "resolution" (not an Art 288 act) fixing the Member States' negotiating position for an international transport agreement and intended to bind them. (d) A Commission recommendation. (2 points)
cards.a:
(b) and (c) can be challenged; (a) and (d) cannot.
• Test: act intended to produce binding legal effects, whatever its form (ERTA, 22/70; IBM, 60/81); Art 263(1) TFEU excludes recommendations/opinions.
• (a) preparatory, not final → no (IBM).
• (b) binding decision (Art 288(4) TFEU) → yes.
• (c) intended to bind → yes (ERTA).
• (d) not binding (Art 288(5)) → no.

cards.q: In January Tecno complained to the Commission that a dominant competitor abuses its position (Art 102 TFEU). In June it sends a formal letter calling on the Commission to decide on the complaint. By the end of August there is still no reply. (a) Which action is available, until when, and before which court? (b) What if the Commission had rejected the complaint by letter in July? (c) What can the Court order? (3 points)
cards.a:
(a) Failure to act, Art 265 TFEU, General Court (Art 256(1)); (b) annulment, Art 263(4); (c) declaration only.
• Art 265(2): June letter = call to act → Commission had two months (ended August) → sue within two further months: same day in October (+10 days distance).
• Art 265(3): complainant entitled to a decision (Art 7 Reg 773/2004) → standing.
• (b) Rejection = definition of position → Art 265 inadmissible; Tecno (addressee) challenges it under Art 263(4).
• (c) Commission must then decide (Art 266), content not dictated.

cards.q: The Swedish tax authority imposes tax surcharges (administrative penalties) on Mr Hans for false VAT and income-tax returns. He is later prosecuted for tax fraud on the same facts and invokes ne bis in idem (Art 50 Charter). Sweden argues the Charter does not apply, because the national laws were not adopted to transpose EU law. (a) Does the Charter apply? (b) What follows for the national court? (3 points)
cards.a:
(a) Yes, for VAT — the penalties implement Union law (Åkerberg Fransson, C-617/10); (b) the court must apply Art 50 Charter, disapplying conflicting national law.
• Art 51(1) Charter: "implementing Union law" = acting within the scope of EU law.
• VAT penalties serve the VAT Directive and Art 325 TFEU → within scope, whatever the transposing intent.
• Income tax: outside EU law → only national rights/ECHR.
• Art 50 applies only if the surcharge is criminal (Engel criteria); duplication justifiable under Art 52(1) (Menci, C-524/15).

cards.q: German law requires fruit liqueurs to contain at least 25% alcohol, so the French "Cassis de Dijon" (15–20%), lawfully produced and marketed in France, cannot be sold in Germany. Germany argues the rule applies equally to domestic and imported liqueurs and protects consumers and health. Assess this under the free movement of goods and explain the principle of mutual recognition. (3 points)
cards.a:
The rule is a measure having equivalent effect (Art 34 TFEU) that cannot be justified.
• Dassonville (8/74): any rule capable of hindering intra-EU trade, directly or indirectly, actually or potentially = MEQR, even if indistinctly applicable.
• Cassis de Dijon (120/78), rule of reason: obstacles accepted only if necessary for mandatory requirements (consumer protection, public health, fair trading) and proportionate.
• Application: health fails; labelling suffices → disproportionate.
• Mutual recognition: goods lawfully produced and marketed in one Member State may in principle be sold in all others.

cards.q: Deborah, a British national (the UK was then a Member State), wants to do her paid preparatory service as a trainee teacher at a German state school. She is refused, because German law reserves trainee civil-servant status to Germans. Germany invokes the "public service" exception in Article 45(4) TFEU. (a) Is Deborah a "worker"? (b) Does Article 45(4) apply? (3 points)
cards.a:
(a) Yes; (b) No — trainee teaching is not a public-service post, so the refusal breaches Art 45(2) TFEU (Lawrie-Blum, 66/85).
• Worker (autonomous EU concept): services for and under the direction of another, for remuneration (Lawrie-Blum); genuine and effective, not marginal (Levin, 53/81) → paid traineeship qualifies.
• Art 45(4) TFEU: construed narrowly and functionally, only posts involving public powers and safeguarding general state interests (Commission v Belgium, 149/79); civil-servant status irrelevant → teachers not covered.
• Result: direct nationality discrimination, Art 45(2) TFEU; no Art 45(3) justification.

cards.q: Distinguish the freedom to provide services from the freedom of establishment and from the free movement of workers, and apply it to: (a) a German lawyer who, from his Stuttgart office, regularly travels to Milan to represent clients but has no office there; (b) the same lawyer opening a permanent office in Milan; (c) an Austrian travelling to Italy for medical treatment. (3 points)
cards.a:
(a) Services (Arts 56–57 TFEU); (b) establishment (Art 49 TFEU); (c) passive freedom to receive services (Art 56 TFEU).
• Workers, Art 45: employed, under subordination. Establishment, Art 49: self-employed, stable and continuous activity from a fixed base. Services, Art 57: self-employed, temporary, for remuneration; residual (Art 57(1)).
• (a) temporary (duration, regularity, periodicity, continuity), no fixed base in Milan → services; some infrastructure allowed (Gebhard, C-55/94).
• (b) permanent office → establishment (Gebhard).
• (c) recipients are protected too (Luisi and Carbone, 286/82 and 26/83).

cards.q: Two car manufacturers agree to develop EV battery technology jointly and share the patents. A third company, with 70% of the EU market for charging software, refuses to license its interface to competitors and grants loyalty rebates. Explain Article 101(3) and Article 102 TFEU and apply them in outline. (3 points)
cards.a:
The R&D agreement may be exempt under Art 101(3) TFEU; the 70% firm presumably abuses dominance (Art 102 TFEU, no exemption).
• Art 101(3): four conditions: progress, fair share to consumers, only indispensable restrictions, no elimination of competition; legal exception (Art 1(2) Reg 1/2003), burden on the firms (Art 2).
• Art 102: dominance = independence from competitors and customers (United Brands, 27/76); >50% → presumed (AKZO, C-62/86); dominance itself lawful.
• Abuse affecting inter-state trade: refusal to license, exceptionally (Microsoft, T-201/04); loyalty rebates (Hoffmann-La Roche, 85/76; Intel, C-413/14 P).

cards.q: Rudy, a French student in his fourth year at a Belgian university, supported himself during the first three years. He then applies for the Belgian "minimex" (minimum subsistence allowance), which Belgian students in his situation receive. Belgium refuses because he is neither Belgian nor a worker. Can Rudy rely on EU primary law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Yes — as a lawfully resident Union citizen he can rely on Art 18 with Arts 20–21 TFEU; the refusal is nationality discrimination (Grzelczyk, C-184/99).
• Art 20(1): Union citizenship = fundamental status of Member State nationals; Art 21(1): right to reside, subject to secondary-law limits.
• Art 18: lawful residence brings him within the Treaties' scope (Martínez Sala, C-85/96).
• Directive 2004/38: Art 7(1)(c) resources, sickness insurance; Art 24(2) exceptions (first three months, study aid) not applicable; no automatic loss of residence for claiming assistance (Art 14(3)).

cards.q: The Council votes on three Commission proposals under the ordinary legislative procedure (27 Member States). Was each adopted? (a) 16 Member States representing 63% of the EU population vote in favour, the other 11 against. (b) 14 Member States representing 72% of the population vote in favour. (c) 24 Member States representing 53% of the population vote in favour; the three most populous states (about 47%) vote against. (3 points)
cards.a:
(a) Not adopted, (b) not adopted, (c) adopted.
• OLP → QMV (Art 16(3) TEU); on a Commission proposal Art 16(4) TEU: at least 55% of members, at least 15, representing at least 65% of the population.
• (a) 16 states met, but 63% < 65% → not adopted.
• (b) 72% met, but 14 < 15 states → not adopted.
• (c) 53% < 65%, but a blocking minority needs at least four members (Art 16(4) subpara 2); only three oppose → QMV deemed attained → adopted.

cards.q: After the European elections, the alliance 'Alpha' becomes the largest group in the European Parliament; its lead candidate (Spitzenkandidat) is Mr Berger. The European Council, by qualified majority, instead proposes Ms Lind, who was not a lead candidate. (a) Is this lawful? (b) Describe the further steps until the Commission takes office. (c) What happens if the Parliament rejects Ms Lind? (4 points)
cards.a:
(a) Lawful — the European Council must only 'take into account' the elections; Spitzenkandidat = political practice, not law.
• Art 17(7) subpara 1 TEU: QMV proposal, no duty to nominate a lead candidate.
• (b) EP elects her by a majority of its component members (subpara 1).
• Council, by common accord with her, adopts the list of Commissioners from Member States' suggestions (subpara 2); European Council appoints High Representative by QMV with her agreement (Art 18(1)).
• EP hearings → EP vote of consent on the college → European Council appoints by QMV (subpara 3).
• (c) New candidate by QMV within one month, same procedure (subpara 1) → EP veto only.

cards.q: After a census Germany's population has grown. Germany demands 110 seats in the European Parliament, Malta insists on keeping its 6 seats, and the European Council decides by qualified majority to enlarge the Parliament to 760 members. Assess the legality. What does 'degressive proportionality' mean? (3 points)
cards.a:
Unlawful (except Malta's 6 seats) — Art 14(2) TEU.
• Subpara 1: max 750 MEPs plus the President; per state min 6, max 96 → 110 for Germany and 760 in total excluded; Malta's 6 = lawful minimum.
• Degressive proportionality: larger states get more seats, but each of their MEPs represents more citizens.
• Subpara 2: composition fixed by the European Council unanimously, on the EP's initiative and with its consent → QMV insufficient.
• Higher caps only by Treaty amendment (Art 48 TEU).

cards.q: Assign each innovation to the correct treaty and give the year it entered into force: (1) Union citizenship, Economic and Monetary Union and the 'three pillars'; (2) incorporation of the Schengen acquis and the sanction procedure for breaches of the Union's values; (3) institutional reform preparing the 2004 enlargement and the preventive 'clear risk' mechanism; (4) a legally binding Charter of Fundamental Rights, legal personality of the Union and a withdrawal clause. (4 points)
cards.a:
(1) Maastricht 1993, (2) Amsterdam 1999, (3) Nice 2003, (4) Lisbon 2009.
• (1) Treaty of Maastricht (TEU), signed 1992, in force 1 Nov 1993: EU on three pillars (EC, CFSP, JHA), Union citizenship, EMU.
• (2) Treaty of Amsterdam, signed 1997, in force 1 May 1999: Schengen integrated into EU law, sanction procedure (today Art 7(2)–(3) TEU).
• (3) Treaty of Nice, signed 2001, in force 1 Feb 2003: votes reweighted and Commission size reformed for enlargement, preventive mechanism (today Art 7(1) TEU).
• (4) Treaty of Lisbon, signed 2007, in force 1 Dec 2009: Charter binding (Art 6(1) TEU), legal personality (Art 47 TEU), withdrawal (Art 50 TEU), pillars abolished (Art 1(3) TEU).

cards.q: Explain the principle of sincere cooperation (loyalty). Where is it laid down, what obligations does it contain, and give three examples of how the Court of Justice has used it. (3 points)
cards.a:
Laid down in Art 4(3) TEU; it binds the Union and the Member States.
• Subpara 1: mutual assistance in full mutual respect.
• Subpara 2 (positive): any appropriate measure to fulfil obligations from the Treaties and EU acts.
• Subpara 3 (negative): facilitate the Union's tasks, refrain from measures jeopardising its objectives.
• Case law: consistent interpretation (von Colson 14/83); effective, proportionate, dissuasive sanctions (Greek Maize 68/88); no measures seriously compromising a directive's result before its deadline (Inter-Environnement Wallonie C-129/96); state liability (Francovich C-6/90).

cards.q: Name the categories of Union competences, their legal consequences and give two examples of each. Why can an act never be based on Art 3 TFEU itself? (4 points)
cards.a:
Five categories (Art 2–6 TFEU); Art 3 only classifies — legal basis is the policy chapter, e.g. Art 103 for competition, not Art 3(1)(b) (Art 2(6)).
• Exclusive (Art 2(1), 3): only the Union legislates; Member States only if empowered or to implement Union acts → customs union, commercial policy.
• Shared (Art 2(2), 4): Member States act where the Union has not (pre-emption) → internal market, environment.
• Coordination (Art 2(3), 5): Member States coordinate economic/employment policies within Union arrangements → guidelines (Art 121, 148).
• CFSP (Art 2(4) TFEU; Art 24 TEU): mostly unanimity, no legislative acts → sanctions, CSDP missions.
• Supporting (Art 2(5), 6): no supersession, no harmonisation → health, culture.

cards.q: Which Art 288 TFEU instrument should the Union use, and why, to (a) lay down identical roaming-charge rules applying immediately to all operators in all Member States, (b) oblige Member States to guarantee minimum paid annual leave while leaving them the choice of how to implement it, (c) fine a specific company for a cartel, (d) encourage Member States to raise vaccination rates without any obligation? (3 points)
cards.a:
(a) Regulation, (b) directive, (c) decision, (d) recommendation.
• (a) Art 288(2) TFEU: general application, binding in its entirety, directly applicable → uniform rules without transposition.
• (b) Art 288(3): binding as to the result, choice of form and methods left to national authorities → transposition by a deadline.
• (c) Art 288(4): binding in its entirety; with addressees, binding only on them → individual case (Commission cartel fine under Reg 1/2003).
• (d) Art 288(5): recommendations have no binding force → soft law (Art 292 TFEU).

cards.q: An equal-treatment directive prohibits compulsory retirement of women earlier than men. The deadline has expired; State Tarvia has not transposed it. Three women are forced to retire at 60, men at 65. Their employers: (a) Tarvian Railways plc, wholly state-owned, running the rail network under a statutory monopoly; (b) Guarantee Fund Ltd, privately owned, entrusted by statute with compensating victims of uninsured drivers and entitled to collect compulsory levies from motor insurers; (c) a private supermarket chain. Against which employers can they rely on the directive? (4 points)
cards.a:
Against (a) and (b) as emanations of the state; not against (c).
• Clear, precise, unconditional prohibition, deadline expired → vertical direct effect, also against the state as employer (Marshall I 152/84).
• Emanation: body under state authority or control, OR entrusted with a public-interest task with special powers — not cumulative (Foster C-188/89; Farrell C-413/15).
• (a) State-owned, public service under statutory monopoly → emanation.
• (b) Private, but statutory public-interest task + special powers (compulsory levies) → emanation (Farrell).
• (c) Horizontal → no direct effect of directives (Art 288(3) TFEU; Faccini Dori C-91/92); only consistent interpretation, arguably Arts 21, 23 Charter (Egenberger), Francovich claim against Tarvia.

cards.q: The Austrian Verwaltungsgerichtshof (VwGH), whose decisions cannot be appealed, must interpret a term in the VAT Directive. Must it refer if (a) the CJEU has already answered an identical question in a German case; (b) there is no CJEU case law and the VwGH finds the answer "obvious", but a Dutch supreme court has interpreted the term differently; (c) the question is irrelevant to the outcome; (d) the question concerns the validity of the directive, which the VwGH considers invalid? (4 points)
cards.a:
(a) No, (b) yes, (c) no, (d) yes.
• Art 267(3) TFEU: a last-instance court must refer questions necessary for its decision unless a CILFIT (283/81) exception applies.
• (a) Acte éclairé — materially identical question already decided (Da Costa 28-30/62) → no duty (may still refer).
• (b) Acte clair only if the answer is equally obvious to other Member States' courts and the CJEU; a plausible divergent reading by another supreme court excludes that → must refer (Consorzio Italian Management C-561/19).
• (c) Irrelevant → no duty (only questions necessary for judgment, Art 267(2)).
• (d) National courts cannot invalidate EU acts → must refer; CILFIT exceptions do not apply (Foto-Frost 314/85).

(d) The question concerns the validity of the directive, which the VwGH considers invalid. (4 points)

cards.q: An importer asks a German first-instance fiscal court to suspend a customs-duty demand based on a Commission regulation that the importer considers invalid for breach of proportionality. The court shares these doubts. (a) May the court declare the regulation invalid and annul the demand? (b) May it at least suspend enforcement until a ruling is given? (3 points)
cards.a:
(a) No — only the CJEU can declare an EU act invalid; (b) yes, under strict EU-law conditions.
• (a) Art 267(1)(b) TFEU: the CJEU rules on validity; national courts at any instance may reject, but not uphold, a plea of invalidity → must refer (Foto-Frost 314/85).
• (b) Suspension allowed if: serious doubts on validity and the court refers (unless already pending); urgency — serious, irreparable damage; due account of the Union's interest; respect for EU court rulings on the act (Zuckerfabrik C-143/88 and C-92/89; Atlanta C-465/93).
